title: Understanding the Experience of the Visually Impaired towards a Multi-Sensorial Architectural Design
research_question: To holistically understand the world of the visually impaired as an attempt to extract the qualities of space that accommodate their needs, and to show the importance of multi-sensory, holistic designs for the blind.

participants.description: 5 visually impaired children (ages 1-4, 3 congenitally blind, 2 low visual acuity), 1 formerly blind 24-year-old Egyptian (blind for 18 years), 1 blind architect (lost sight at 45), 1 author of books on blindness. Authors also participated in blind-folded experiences.
participants.recruitment: Not explicitly stated for all, but children were observed in an NGO in Cairo, Egypt. A.A. was interviewed in Cairo, Egypt. Downey and Hull's experiences were from literature.

stimuli_or_exposures.description: Old Cairo (sound-walk), Bauhaus University building (indoor exercise), Weimar city (outdoor park walk, city center), Kimbell Art Museum, various airports.
Montessori materials (duplicates of wood, metal, plastic, concrete; play dough; rods; rings for stereognosis and scale/proportion training).
Natural elements (sun, water, air, leaves, grass, plants, rain) and their associated sensory qualities (heat, sound, smell, flow).
Architectural materials (floor pavers, handrails, walls, carpets, concrete, wood, plaster, paint) and their associated haptic, acoustic, and olfactory qualities.

measures.construct: Understanding of light intensity and atmosphere
Acoustic experience and understanding of contours
Perceived freshness and blending with nature
Material identification by texture, temperature, weight, and smell
Understanding of space form, dimensions, and atmosphere
Perceived liveliness vs. deadness of space
Development of mental maps and spatial understanding
Object size, shape, and form perception
Spatial perception and distance understanding through hearing
Mental representation and environmental understanding through smell
Orientation, mobility, and familiar environment recognition

findings.antecedent: Outside environment (breezes, sounds of breeze through leaves, birds)
findings.consequent: Perceived dynamism and enjoyment of the environment
findings.mechanism: Multisensory input from nature creates a dynamic and engaging experience.
findings.quote: The outside is so much more dynamic. There are breezes, there are the sounds of a breeze through the leaves in the tree, or birds off in the distance.

findings.antecedent: Sun heat on skin and airflow
findings.consequent: Understanding of light intensity and surrounding atmosphere
findings.mechanism: Passive haptic perception (thermal and tactile) provides information about environmental conditions.
findings.quote: Being totally blind, the only way that I could feel the light intensity in a space was feeling the sun heat on my skin, the sun heat and air flow approach me

findings.antecedent: Rain (sound of splashing, drumming on different surfaces)
findings.consequent: Continuous acoustic experience and understanding of environmental contours (e.g., lawn, hill curvature)
findings.mechanism: Acoustic cues from rain interacting with surfaces provide information about topography and material.
findings.quote: Through the sound of splashing rain, I can interpret the contours of the lawn, which rises to the right in a little hill.

findings.antecedent: Park environment (birds, water stream, air through grass/leaves, plant/water smells)
findings.consequent: Perceived calmness and a rich multisensory experience
findings.mechanism: Natural elements provide diverse and pleasant sensory inputs, contributing to a sense of calm and engagement.
findings.quote: Entering the park from the main street and feeling the sudden calmness, only hearing birds, water stream, air penetrating through grass and leaves while smelling plants and water.

findings.consequent: Recognition of tree shaded areas
findings.mechanism: Thermal sensation on the skin provides cues about environmental features like shade.
findings.quote: The sunlight warmth was the way we recognized the tree shaded areas

findings.antecedent: Smell of greens, flowers, and water
findings.consequent: Perceived freshness
findings.mechanism: Olfactory cues from natural elements contribute to a sense of freshness.
findings.quote: smell of greens, flowers and water was strong, felt like the smell of freshness.

findings.antecedent: Interaction with water stream (smell, splashing on rocks, feeling water through fingers)
findings.consequent: Sense of blending in with natural elements
findings.mechanism: Multisensory engagement with water fosters a feeling of connection to nature.
findings.quote: The special smell of water stream blending in with the soil and rocks, splashing on the rocks then to our skin felt like a way of blending in with the natural elements in the park.

findings.antecedent: Engagement with nature (for visually impaired children)
findings.consequent: Helpful tool in learning development
findings.mechanism: Nature provides a rich, low-demand sensory environment conducive to learning and attention restoration.
findings.quote: Studies about visually impaired children recommend engagement with nature as a helpful tool in their learning development

findings.antecedent: Difference in floor pavers texture (e.g., underground)
findings.consequent: Understanding of location and orientation
findings.mechanism: Haptic feedback from floor textures provides crucial cues for spatial navigation and place identification.
findings.quote: the difference in floor pavers used in the underground helped him understand the location he was standing on, which made it easy for him to understand his location and orientation.

findings.antecedent: Handrail material (warm wood with old wood smell vs. cool metal with plaster/paint)
findings.consequent: Material recognition and spatial context understanding
findings.mechanism: Multisensory cues (haptic temperature, texture, olfactory) contribute to material identification and memory of place.
findings.quote: two different handrails, the main one felt warm with an old wood smell, and the other one was cool made of metal and covered in plaster and paint. The smell of the staircase made of old-wood was dominant

findings.antecedent: Floor textures (rough pavers vs. smooth flooring)
findings.consequent: Changes in perception and walking difficulty (rough pavers harder to walk on)
findings.mechanism: Haptic feedback from floor surfaces directly impacts motor control and perceived ease of movement, influencing spatial perception.
findings.quote: Rough pavers were harder to walk on, so after a while they had to sit and rest from walking.

findings.antecedent: Smell of stone from old buildings, water reacting with stones, and ground concrete pavers
findings.consequent: Material recognition
findings.mechanism: Olfactory cues are strongly associated with specific materials and their context, aiding recognition.
findings.quote: participants recognized the smell of stone from old buildings while walking next to them from and the scent of water reacting with the stones of buildings and with the ground concrete pavers.

findings.antecedent: Contrast between rough asphalt, smooth lawn, and concrete pavers (outdoor surfaces)
findings.consequent: Spatial recognition
findings.mechanism: Distinct haptic feedback from different surfaces provides clear cues for distinguishing spatial areas.
findings.quote: The contrast between the rough asphalt and the smooth lawn was very recognized, then again from the smooth lawn to the concrete pavers at the city center.

findings.antecedent: Montessori activity using duplicates of wood, metal, plastic, and concrete
findings.consequent: Material recognition by texture, temperature, and weight
findings.mechanism: Active haptic exploration and comparison of material properties (texture, temperature, weight) facilitate material identification.
findings.quote: They also learn to identify different materials through a Montessori activity where they use duplicates of wood, metal, plastic and concrete, recognizing them from their texture, temperature and weight

findings.antecedent: Acoustics of a space (e.g., Kimbell Art Museum vaults)
findings.consequent: Understanding of space form and dimensions, perceived delight
findings.mechanism: Auditory cues, including reverberation and sound propagation, provide information about spatial geometry and evoke emotional responses.
findings.quote: I really wanted to hear what the vaults were like, and see if I could understand the form of those spaces through sound... I could hear the whole length extend out in either direction. I could also hear the delicate, crisp sound of people walking on crushed gravel pathways nearby and the sound of a fountain. It was hard to resist. You just wanted to go there, because it sounded like such a delightful space

findings.consequent: Understanding of space, distance, and height
findings.mechanism: Hearing provides crucial spatial cues for perceiving depth and verticality.
findings.quote: Hearing architecture is how he imagined and understood the space, it is how he imagined the height because hearing is the sense of distance

findings.consequent: Understanding of space wideness and crowdedness
findings.mechanism: Echo characteristics provide information about the volume and occupancy of a space.
findings.quote: Echo used to play a very important role in understanding the surrounding space, it made me understand the space wideness and how crowded it is

findings.antecedent: Ceiling height (intermediate vs. low vs. high)
findings.consequent: Echo characteristics and ease of echo tracking (low ceilings result in high echoes, high ceilings make it hard to track echo)
findings.mechanism: Ceiling height influences sound reflection and reverberation, affecting the utility of echo for spatial perception.
findings.quote: high echo means a space is wide and empty and vice versa. I usually prefer ceilings with intermediate heights, low ceilings result in high echoes, while high ceilings make it hard to track echo

findings.consequent: Perceived deadness and lack of liveliness in a space (due to lack of footfall sounds)
findings.mechanism: Lack of ambient human sounds reduces perceived activity and vitality of a space.
findings.quote: Earlier this week, I traveled through some airports that are carpeted everywhere. It was dead and flat. You never heard footfalls or roller bags, you didn't hear the liveliness of the space.

findings.antecedent: Multisensory exploration (cane, hands, feet, clapping, smelling materials)
findings.consequent: Development of a mental map and easier understanding of a place when revisited
findings.mechanism: Integrating information from multiple senses allows for comprehensive spatial encoding and mental map formation, facilitating future navigation.
findings.quote: I walk around, touch the surroundings with my cane, hands and feet, hit several objects while walking, clap to feel the echo, and thus, the wideness of space, and I smell the materials and this is how I develop a mental map of the surroundings, making it easier to understand the place when revisited.

findings.antecedent: Specific smells (perfumes, incenses, bakeries, coffee) along a walk
findings.consequent: Memory and recognition of specific areas
findings.mechanism: Olfactory cues are strongly linked to memory and can serve as powerful contextual anchors for place recognition.
findings.quote: The scent along the walk was important as participants remembered specific areas through the smell of perfumes, incenses, bakeries and coffee.

findings.antecedent: Touching surrounding walls (e.g., historic mosque, old houses)
findings.consequent: Identification of location and buildings through cognitive mapping and touching
findings.mechanism: Haptic exploration of architectural surfaces provides direct information for building a mental representation and recognizing specific structures.
findings.quote: it was very important to touch the surrounding walls to be able to identify the location and buildings like El Hakim historic mosque and old houses were identified through both cognitive mapping and touching.

findings.consequent: Identification of window locations without direct touch
findings.mechanism: Passive thermal sensation (heat on skin) provides non-haptic cues for environmental features.
findings.quote: the sunlight penetrating through the windows was felt on our skin and its warmth made it easy to indicate the locations of windows without approaching and touching them.

findings.antecedent: Airflow (e.g., near double-height staircase, main entrance)
findings.consequent: Spatial recognition and understanding of transitions
findings.mechanism: Tactile sensation of airflow provides cues about open spaces, changes in volume, and proximity to entrances.
findings.quote: the airflow felt higher when approaching the double-heighted staircase area and moving towards the main entrance where the door opens and closes.

findings.antecedent: Arm and feet exploration (creating virtual personal space)
findings.consequent: Recognition of walls, doors, chairs, tables, and other objects
findings.mechanism: Active haptic exploration with limbs allows for direct object identification and spatial mapping within a personal reach.
findings.quote: children create a virtual personal space around them with their arms... arms and feet are used to recognize walls, doors, chairs, table and all other objects.

findings.consequent: Learning to identify and avoid obstacles while walking
findings.mechanism: Direct haptic interaction with obstacles provides immediate feedback for developing avoidance strategies and motor predictions.
findings.quote: learning how to identify and avoid obstacles while walking, and this is achieved by touching an obstructing rope and reacting to it

findings.consequent: Congruence between imagined and real object properties (except for colors), and multisensory object recognition
findings.mechanism: Prior haptic and other sensory experiences form robust mental representations that align with newly acquired visual information, with color being a novel attribute.
findings.quote: It was not different, it was the same but with colors... When I opened my eyes, and started seeing, I was amazed with colors... When I saw the table, I knew that this was a table because I remember touching and feeling it, just like seeing it.

findings.consequent: Perception of object size and shape (stereognosis)
findings.mechanism: Active manipulation and tactile feedback from objects allow for the construction of their three-dimensional properties.
findings.quote: Stereognosis is developed to train visually impaired children to perceive the size and shape of objects through their hands.

findings.antecedent: Play dough shaping into spheres, cubes, rods and touching them
findings.consequent: Object name and form recognition
findings.mechanism: Active haptic manipulation and tactile feedback reinforce the understanding and naming of object forms.
findings.quote: children shape the play dough into spheres, cubes and rods. Once they form the shape, they touch it and name it; this activity assures the object's name.

findings.antecedent: Haptic exploration of scaled objects (rods, rings)
findings.consequent: Understanding of size and scale
findings.mechanism: Direct haptic comparison and arrangement of objects of varying sizes facilitate the conceptual understanding of scale and proportion.
findings.quote: visually impaired children learn about scale and proportion by touching rods of different scales and arranging them from longest to shortest

findings.consequent: Perception of surrounding environment (nature, space, materials)
findings.mechanism: Haptic feedback, both self-initiated (active) and externally received (passive), is a primary channel for environmental information.
findings.quote: Haptic feedback is one of the main channels through which the visually impaired perceive their surrounding environment. Through the touching sense, visually impaired people can feel the nature surrounding them, feel the space surrounding them, recognize space and recognize materials.

findings.antecedent: Active touching (moving, exerting pressure, pushing, pulling)
findings.consequent: Identification of material texture and contours of the ground
findings.mechanism: Kinesthetic and tactile feedback from active exploration provides detailed information about surface properties and spatial forms.
findings.quote: Materials texture identification and feeling, perceiving the contours of the ground underneath were considered active tactile stimulants.

findings.antecedent: Kinesthetic active touching (work with muscles/joints, touching)
findings.consequent: Recognition of object form and parameters
findings.mechanism: Integrated sensorimotor feedback from active manipulation allows for comprehensive understanding of object properties.
findings.quote: Kinesthetic involves work with muscles and joints along with the touching; form recognition, touching and feeling the parameters of an object were considered forms of kinesthetic active touching

findings.antecedent: Passive touching (unexpected tactile events, heat sensation, airflow, water splashing)
findings.consequent: Perception of surrounding nature, light intensity, and environmental conditions
findings.mechanism: Unanticipated tactile and thermal inputs provide direct, immediate information about the environment.
findings.quote: Passive touching happens when a tactile event occurs that is unexpectedly reaching the body. The interaction of body with the surrounding nature was considered a kind of passive touching, heat sensation on the skin when the visually impaired feel the light intensity, feeling the nature surrounding, air flow on the skin along with natural splashing water.

findings.antecedent: Tactile contrast between two materials (e.g., for a visual border)
findings.consequent: Clear distinction of materials and spatial boundaries
findings.mechanism: Distinct haptic properties provide clear cues for differentiating materials and defining spatial transitions.
findings.quote: A contrast between two materials should be clear in its texture

findings.consequent: Perception and understanding of the surrounding world, providing a three-dimensional distant and near atmosphere
findings.mechanism: Auditory cues are crucial for constructing a spatial mental model, especially for distance and depth.
findings.quote: Hearing is crucial for the visually impaired to perceive and understand their surrounding world, it provides a three-dimensional distant and near atmosphere.

findings.consequent: Preference and blending with the surrounding environment
findings.mechanism: Natural soundscapes are often perceived as pleasant and facilitate a sense of connection to the environment.
findings.quote: The sound of nature is usually preferred to by the visually impaired because it makes them blend with the surrounding environment

findings.consequent: Perceived liveliness and excitement in a space
findings.mechanism: Auditory cues of human activity contribute to the perceived vitality and social atmosphere of a space.
findings.quote: The term "dynamic place” was mentioned by Chris Downey while describing a place with sounds of activity, unlike "carpeted places" where he does not hear the liveliness of the place, and so he described it as dead.

findings.consequent: Material and spatial recognition
findings.mechanism: Echo characteristics provide information about surface properties and spatial dimensions, aiding recognition.
findings.quote: Sound echo also helps in materials and spatial recognition

findings.consequent: Perception of material and spatial properties
findings.mechanism: Auditory feedback from cane tapping provides information about surface materials and spatial boundaries.
findings.quote: Instead of doing a 'walk-through, we create a 'tap-through, so you hear what it's like when you tap your cane throughout the building.

findings.consequent: Building a mental representation of the surrounding environment
findings.mechanism: Olfactory input is directly processed by limbic structures, contributing to spatial memory and mental mapping.
findings.quote: The study shows that sense of smell helps visually impaired people build a mental representation of their surrounding environment.

findings.consequent: Place identification and memory recall when revisited
findings.mechanism: Olfactory cues serve as strong memory triggers, enabling recognition of familiar places.
findings.quote: Places were easily identified with smell because every place has a certain smell that can be recalled when revisited

findings.antecedent: Material smells (wood, plaster, paint, damp concrete)
findings.consequent: Material identification and recognition of material age
findings.mechanism: Distinct olfactory profiles of materials, including those associated with aging, aid in their identification.
findings.quote: materials are identified from their smell, the smell of wood was easily distinguished, the smell of plaster and paint, damp concrete, and moreover, the age of material was recognized.

findings.antecedent: Harmony between haptic, auditory, and olfactory perceptions
findings.consequent: Successful orientation, mobility, and recognition of familiar environments
findings.mechanism: Synchronized multisensory input provides coherent environmental information, facilitating cognitive mapping and navigation.
findings.quote: For successful orientation and mobility of the visually impaired, a harmony between haptic, auditory and olfactory perceptions is achieved and that is how they easily recognize familiar environments, the senses synchronization.

findings.consequent: Enhanced cognitive mapping skills and ability to move safely and independently
findings.mechanism: Targeted training across multiple senses improves the ability to form and utilize mental representations for navigation and autonomy.
findings.quote: visually impaired children learn to enhance their cognitive mapping skills by using all their senses to be able to move safely and independently.

findings.consequent: Perception of nature and spatial properties
findings.mechanism: Tactile sensation of airflow provides information about open spaces and environmental conditions.
findings.quote: Airflow -> Haptic, Auditory

findings.consequent: Perception of nature
findings.mechanism: Thermal sensation provides direct information about the presence of sunlight and associated natural elements.
findings.quote: Sunlight heat sensation -> Haptic

findings.consequent: Perception of nature
findings.mechanism: Olfactory cues directly inform about the presence and type of natural elements.
findings.quote: Smell of natural elements -> Olfactory

findings.consequent: Perception of nature
findings.mechanism: Auditory cues from environmental atmosphere and activities contribute to the overall perception of nature.
findings.quote: Atmosphere and activities -> Auditory

findings.consequent: Material texture perception
findings.mechanism: Tactile feedback from surface irregularities provides direct information about material texture.
findings.quote: Material Roughness and smoothness -> Haptic

findings.consequent: Material texture perception
findings.mechanism: Thermal properties of materials are perceived through touch, contributing to material identification.
findings.quote: Material Temperature -> Haptic

findings.consequent: Material recognition
findings.mechanism: Multisensory cues (haptic, auditory, olfactory) contribute to the recognition of material forms.
findings.quote: Form recognition -> Haptic, Auditory, Olfactory

findings.consequent: Spatial understanding
findings.mechanism: Direct haptic interaction with the environment provides fundamental information for spatial awareness.
findings.quote: Touch and feel recognition -> Haptic

findings.consequent: Spatial understanding
findings.mechanism: Haptic feedback from ground variations provides critical information for understanding spatial layout and movement.
findings.quote: Ground Topography and contours -> Haptic

findings.consequent: Spatial understanding
findings.mechanism: Auditory cues, particularly echoes and sound propagation, are used to infer spatial dimensions.
findings.quote: Width and height -> Auditory

findings.consequent: Spatial understanding
findings.mechanism: Multisensory cues (haptic, auditory, olfactory) are integrated to form a comprehensive understanding of spatial properties.
findings.quote: Spatial properties -> Haptic, Auditory, Olfactory

findings.consequent: Spatial recognition
findings.mechanism: Multisensory cues (haptic, auditory, olfactory) are integrated for effective spatial recognition.
findings.quote: Spatial recognition -> Haptic, Auditory, Olfactory

mechanisms: Intersubjectivity: Shared understanding built from combining different perspectives (blind individuals, architects, children, personal experience).
Multisensory integration: Visually impaired individuals rely on tactile (active and passive), acoustic, and olfactory cues to construct a holistic mental representation of their environment.
Haptic feedback: Direct physical interaction with surfaces and objects provides information about texture, temperature, form, and spatial boundaries.
Auditory spatial cues: Echoes, sound propagation, and distinct sounds (e.g., rain, footfalls) provide information about space dimensions, materials, and activity.
Olfactory memory and recognition: Unique smells of places and materials serve as strong cues for identification, memory recall, and emotional association.
Cognitive mapping: Multisensory information is processed, organized, and stored to build mental maps for orientation, mobility, and independent navigation.
implementation_implications: Architectural designs should prioritize multi-sensory and holistic experiences for the visually impaired, moving beyond visual dominance.
Haptic and aural inclusive designs are essential to create environments that empower visually impaired individuals for independent, safe, and efficient living.
Design should incorporate tactile contrasts in materials (e.g., floor pavers, handrails) to aid in wayfinding and material recognition.
Acoustic design should consider reverberation and soundscapes to provide spatial information and a sense of liveliness, avoiding 'dead' spaces (e.g., heavily carpeted areas).
Natural elements (sunlight warmth, airflow, natural sounds, smells) should be integrated to provide rich sensory cues for environmental understanding and well-being.
Design should facilitate active haptic exploration and provide distinct olfactory cues for place and material identification.

Study Extracted Themes, listing themes, sub-themes, and their corresponding perceptual channels (Haptic, Auditory, Olfactory perception).

limitations: The personal blind-folded experience may not accurately represent the experience of a truly blind person, as the participant still possesses a 'seeing person's brain' (as noted by Hull).
